claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis adenylyl cyclase Rv1625c/Cya is an evolutionary ancestor of the mammalian membrane ACs.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis adenylyl cyclase (AC) Rv1625c/Cya is an evolutionary ancestor of the mammalian membrane ACs and a model system for studies of their structure and function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of the protein being studied.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of Cya bound to a stabilizing nanobody was determined at 3.6 Å resolution.
source: Here, we describe the cryo-EM structure of Cya bound to a stabilizing nanobody at 3.6 Å resolution.
evidence: The resolution is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The TM helices 1–5 form a structurally conserved domain that facilitates the assembly of the helical and catalytic domains.
source: The TM helices 1–5 form a structurally conserved domain that facilitates the assembly of the helical and catalytic domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The TM region contains discrete pockets accessible from the extracellular and cytosolic side of the membrane.
source: The TM region contains discrete pockets accessible from the extracellular and cytosolic side of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 4 with structural analysis.

claim: Neutralization of the negatively charged extracellular pocket Ex1 destabilizes the cytosolic helical domain and reduces the catalytic activity of the enzyme.
source: Neutralization of the negatively charged extracellular pocket Ex1 destabilizes the cytosolic helical domain and reduces the catalytic activity of the enzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing Ex1-5A mutant characterization.

claim: The TM domain acts as a functional component of Cya, guiding the assembly of the catalytic domain and providing the means for direct regulation of catalytic activity in response to extracellular ligands.
source: The TM domain acts as a functional component of Cya, guiding the assembly of the catalytic domain and providing the means for direct regulation of catalytic activity in response to extracellular ligands.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by structural and functional data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Adenylyl cyclases convert molecules of ATP into 3,5-cyclic AMP (cAMP).
source: Adenylyl cyclases (ACs) convert molecules of ATP into 3,5-cyclic AMP (cAMP), a universal second messenger and a master regulator of cellular homeostasis (Linder, 2006).
evidence: This is a well-established fact cited from the literature.

claim: cAMP is a universal second messenger and a master regulator of cellular homeostasis.
source: Adenylyl cyclases (ACs) convert molecules of ATP into 3,5-cyclic AMP (cAMP), a universal second messenger and a master regulator of cellular homeostasis (Linder, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as established knowledge.

claim: In mammalian cells, the membrane-associated ACs generate cAMP upon activation of the cell surface receptors, GPCR, via G protein subunits.
source: In mammalian cells, the membrane-associated ACs (Figure 1A) generate cAMP upon activation of the cell surface receptors, GPCR, via G protein subunits (Sassone-Corsi, 2012), or in some cases by Ca2+/calmodulin (Halls and Cooper, 2011).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as established knowledge about AC regulation.

claim: The nine mammalian membrane ACs (AC1–9) share the topology and domain organization: 12 transmembrane (TM) helices with TM6 and TM12 extending to form a coiled coil of the helical domain (HD), linking the TM bundle to the bipartite catalytic domain.
source: The nine mammalian membrane ACs (AC1–9) share the topology and domain organization: 12 transmembrane (TM) helices with TM6 and TM12 extending to form a coiled coil of the helical domain (HD), linking the TM bundle to the bipartite catalytic domain (Figure 1A; Qi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the full-length bovine AC9 bound to G protein αs subunit revealed the organization of the membrane-integral region of a membrane AC.
source: Recently, we determined the cryo-EM structure of the full-length AC, the bovine AC9 bound to G protein αs subunit, revealing the organization of the membrane-integral region of a membrane AC (Qi et al., 2019).
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors.

claim: The role of the elaborate 12-helical membrane domain in mammalian ACs remains unexplained.
source: Although the structure provided important insights into the mechanism of AC9 auto-regulation, the role of the elaborate 12-helical membrane domain remains unexplained.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the current study.

claim: Rv1625c/Cya is a putative evolutionary ancestor of the mammalian membrane ACs identified in the genome of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: A putative evolutionary ancestor of the mammalian membrane ACs has been identified in the genome of Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Rv1625c, or Cya (Guo et al., 2001; Guo et al., 2005); for simplicity, we refer to this protein as Cya throughout.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Cya is one of the sixteen ACs present in genome of M. tuberculosis.
source: This protein is one of the sixteen ACs present in genome of M. tuberculosis, and one of five ACs predicted to be polytopic membrane proteins (Bai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Cya is one of five ACs predicted to be polytopic membrane proteins in M. tuberculosis.
source: This protein is one of the sixteen ACs present in genome of M. tuberculosis, and one of five ACs predicted to be polytopic membrane proteins (Bai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Cya may be involved in CO2 sensing in M. tuberculosis.
source: The exact function of Cya is not clear, although available evidence indicates that the protein may be involved in CO2 sensing (Townsend et al., 2009) and cholesterol utilization by M. tuberculosis (Johnson et al., 2017; VanderVen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as a potential function.

claim: Cya may be involved in cholesterol utilization by M. tuberculosis.
source: The exact function of Cya is not clear, although available evidence indicates that the protein may be involved in CO2 sensing (Townsend et al., 2009) and cholesterol utilization by M. tuberculosis (Johnson et al., 2017; VanderVen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as a potential function.

claim: Cholesterol utilization during infection by M. tuberculosis is linked to its pathogenesis.
source: Cholesterol utilization during infection by M. tuberculosis is linked to its pathogenesis (Wilburn et al., 2018), indicating a potential role of Cya at some stages of macrophage infection.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The catalytic domain of Cya belongs to the class III AC/guanylyl cyclase (GC) fold, similar to the mammalian membrane ACs.
source: The catalytic domain of Cya belongs to the class III AC/guanylyl cyclase (GC) fold, similar to the mammalian membrane ACs.
evidence: This is stated as a structural classification.

claim: Cya is predicted to include only six TM helices, with TM6 extending into a HD connected to the catalytic domain.
source: Unlike the mammalian ACs, Cya is predicted to include only six TM helices, with TM6 extending into a HD connected to the catalytic domain (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Cya has to dimerize to form a functional unit that resembles the pseudo-heterodimeric fold of the full-length mammalian ACs.
source: The protein has to dimerize to form a functional unit that has been previously presumed to resemble the pseudo-heterodimeric fold of the full-length mammalian ACs (Ketkar et al., 2006; Vercellino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The structure of the M. tuberculosis Cya-soluble domain in monomeric form has been solved using X-ray crystallography.
source: Although the structures of the M. tuberculosis Cya-soluble domain in monomeric form (Ketkar et al., 2006) and that of the homologous M. intracellulare Cya in dimeric form Vercellino et al., 2017 have been solved using X-ray crystallography, a structure of a full-length mycobacterial AC that includes the TM region has not been determined until now.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The structure of the homologous M. intracellulare Cya in dimeric form has been solved using X-ray crystallography.
source: Although the structures of the M. tuberculosis Cya-soluble domain in monomeric form (Ketkar et al., 2006) and that of the homologous M. intracellulare Cya in dimeric form Vercellino et al., 2017 have been solved using X-ray crystallography, a structure of a full-length mycobacterial AC that includes the TM region has not been determined until now.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: A structure of a full-length mycobacterial AC that includes the TM region has not been determined until now.
source: Although the structures of the M. tuberculosis Cya-soluble domain in monomeric form (Ketkar et al., 2006) and that of the homologous M. intracellulare Cya in dimeric form Vercellino et al., 2017 have been solved using X-ray crystallography, a structure of a full-length mycobacterial AC that includes the TM region has not been determined until now.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

claim: Experiments with domain-substituted Cya have suggested that its membrane region may have a regulatory role, potentially acting as a receptor for yet unidentified ligands.
source: Interestingly, experiments with domain-substituted Cya, a presumptive evolutionary ancestor of the mammalian ACs, have suggested that its membrane region may have a regulatory role, potentially acting as a receptor for yet unidentified ligands (Beltz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The full-length M. tuberculosis Cya was expressed in Escherichia coli and purified in digitonin micelles.
source: The full-length M. tuberculosis Cya (Figure 1C) was expressed in Escherichia coli and purified in digitonin micelles using affinity chromatography followed by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: AC activity assays confirmed that the full-length Cya protein was purified in a functional form.
source: AC activity assays confirmed that the full-length protein was purified in a functional form (Figure 1D; Km for Cya was ~80 μM).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Km for full-length Cya is approximately 80 μM.
source: AC activity assays confirmed that the full-length protein was purified in a functional form (Figure 1D; Km for Cya was ~80 μM).
evidence: This is a measured value from activity assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nanobody NB4 had no effect on the catalytic activity of the full-length cyclase.
source: One of these reagents, nanobody 4 (NB4), had no effect on the catalytic activity of the full-length cyclase (Figure 1D), but had a nanomolar affinity for the SOL domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nanobody NB4 had a nanomolar affinity for the SOL domain.
source: One of these reagents, nanobody 4 (NB4), had no effect on the catalytic activity of the full-length cyclase (Figure 1D), but had a nanomolar affinity for the SOL domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The 3D reconstruction revealed the full-length Cya arranged as a dimer bound to three copies of NB4 nanobody.
source: The reconstruction revealed the full-length Cya arranged as a dimer bound to three copies of NB4 nanobody: two copies bound symmetrically to the SOL portions of the Cya dimer, and one asymmetrically bound to the extracellular surface of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Two copies of NB4 bound symmetrically to the SOL portions of the Cya dimer.
source: The reconstruction revealed the full-length Cya arranged as a dimer bound to three copies of NB4 nanobody: two copies bound symmetrically to the SOL portions of the Cya dimer, and one asymmetrically bound to the extracellular surface of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: One copy of NB4 bound asymmetrically to the extracellular surface of Cya.
source: The reconstruction revealed the full-length Cya arranged as a dimer bound to three copies of NB4 nanobody: two copies bound symmetrically to the SOL portions of the Cya dimer, and one asymmetrically bound to the extracellular surface of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The X-ray structure of the Cya-SOL–NB4 complex was solved at 2.1 Å resolution.
source: To visualize the details of the Cya–NB4 interaction, we crystallized the SOL construct in the presence of NB4 and solved the X-ray structure of the complex at 2.1 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The X-ray structure showed an extensive interaction interface between the negatively charged surface of the monomeric SOL domain and the NB4.
source: The structure showed an extensive interaction interface between the negatively charged surface of the monomeric SOL domain and the NB4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is observed in the X-ray structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The crystallized Cya-SOL construct did not form a native-like dimeric form of the enzyme.
source: Interestingly, the crystallized construct did not form a native-like dimeric form of the enzyme, but nevertheless retained the ability to bind to MANT-GTP/Mn2+, with an unusual twist of the MANT-GTP base (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is observed in the X-ray structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The crystallized Cya-SOL construct retained the ability to bind to MANT-GTP/Mn2+.
source: Interestingly, the crystallized construct did not form a native-like dimeric form of the enzyme, but nevertheless retained the ability to bind to MANT-GTP/Mn2+, with an unusual twist of the MANT-GTP base (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is observed in the X-ray structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Masked refinement with C2 symmetry imposed resulted in a 3D reconstruction at 3.57 Å resolution.
source: To improve the resolution of the cryo-EM density map in the regions of highest interest, we masked out the extracellular NB4 density and refined the Cya–NB4 dataset imposing the C2 symmetry. This resulted in a 3D reconstruction at 3.57 Å resolution, which allowed us to reliably trace the polypeptide chain in the cryo-EM density map, covering residues 41–428 of the full-length Cya construct (Figure 1E, F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the cryo-EM data.

claim: The cryo-EM structure covers residues 41–428 of the full-length Cya construct.
source: To improve the resolution of the cryo-EM density map in the regions of highest interest, we masked out the extracellular NB4 density and refined the Cya–NB4 dataset imposing the C2 symmetry. This resulted in a 3D reconstruction at 3.57 Å resolution, which allowed us to reliably trace the polypeptide chain in the cryo-EM density map, covering residues 41–428 of the full-length Cya construct (Figure 1E, F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The 3D reconstruction revealed the previously unresolved portion of the protein, the 6-TM bundle, arranged into a homodimer.
source: Our 3D reconstruction revealed the previously unresolved portion of the protein, the 6-TM bundle, arranged into a homodimer (Figures 1F and 2B, D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 1F and 2B, D.

claim: The SOL portion of Cya adopted a conformation consistent with the previous structure of the SOL domain of M. intracellulare Cya homologue.
source: The SOL portion of the protein, linked to the TM region via the HD, adopted a conformation consistent with our previous structure of the SOL domain of M. intracellulare Cya homologue (Figure 1—figure supplement 5; Vercellino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by comparison with previous structures.

claim: The two nucleotide-binding sites of Cya are occupied with the molecules of MANT-GTP/Mn2+.
source: The two nucleotide-binding sites of Cya are occupied with the molecules of MANT-GTP/Mn2+, which we modelled based on the previous structures and the X-ray structure of SOL–NB4 complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the structure.

claim: The C1 and C2 maps provide no clear evidence of asymmetry in the active site.
source: The C1 and C2 maps provide no clear evidence of asymmetry in the active site, which we have observed in the structure of M. intracellulare Cya (Vercellino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of the cryo-EM maps.

claim: The HD region is believed to be a critical element in the membrane and soluble ACs and GCs, as this region couples the N-terminal regulatory domains to the catalytic function of these proteins.
source: The HD region is believed to be a critical element in the membrane and soluble ACs and GCs, as this region couples the N-terminal regulatory domains to the catalytic function of these proteins (Kang et al., 2019; Scheib et al., 2018; Ohki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: In Cya, the HD extends from the TM6, forming a coiled coil observed in the structures of homologous proteins.
source: In Cya, the HD extends from the TM6 (Figure 2A, B), forming a coiled coil observed in the structures of homologous proteins, including AC9 (Figure 2C; Qi et al., 2019) and sGC (Kang et al., 2019; Figure 3).
evidence: This is observed in the structure and compared with homologous proteins.

claim: The size difference between the HD helix in Cya and the HD1 and HD2 helices in AC9 leads to an ~90° rotation of the corresponding TM regions, relative to the catalytic domains.
source: Interestingly, the size difference between the HD helix in Cya and the HD1 and HD2 helices in AC9 leads to an ~90 rotation of the corresponding TM regions, relative to the catalytic domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The exact structural alignment of the TM domain and the relatively remote catalytic domain may not be a conserved feature of the membrane ACs.
source: This may be an indication that the exact structural alignment of the TM domain and the relatively remote catalytic domain may not be a conserved feature of the membrane ACs.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison between Cya and AC9.

claim: The precise TM–HD and HD–catalytic domain coupling plays the key role in the formation and regulation of the catalytic centre in the membrane AC.
source: Instead, it is likely that the precise TM–HD and HD–catalytic domain coupling plays the key role in the formation and regulation of the catalytic centre in the membrane AC, consistent with the function of the HD as a transducer element in the AC structure (Ziegler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis and supported by citation.

claim: The resolved portion of the Cya N-terminus (residues V41ARRQR46), rich in positively charged residues, is immediately adjacent to the HD region.
source: The resolved portion of the Cya N-terminus (residues V41ARRQR46), rich in positively charged residues, is immediately adjacent to the HD region.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: Early work on Cya identified mutations in the N-terminal region that disrupt the function of the protein.
source: The early work on Cya identified the mutations in this region that disrupt the function of the protein (Vercellino et al., 2017), suggesting that the intact residues in the N-terminus stabilize the HD.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The positively charged residues R43–R44 likely stabilize the negatively charged surface of the HD.
source: The positively charged residues R43–R44 likely stabilize the negatively charged surface of the HD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The TM helices 4, 5, and 6 of Cya form an extensive dimer interface within the membrane.
source: The TM helices 4, 5, and 6 of Cya form an extensive dimer interface within the membrane (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The dimer interface residues, close to the 'core' of the protein, are relatively well conserved among the Cya homologues from Mycobacteria.
source: The dimer interface residues, close to the 'core' of the protein, are relatively well conserved among the Cya homologues from Mycobacteria (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3), with relatively poorly conserved residues in TM1–3.
evidence: This is shown in conservation analysis in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The helices TM1–5 (and TM7–11 for the AC9) form a well defined structural motif.
source: A comparison of the 6-TM bundle of Cya with the corresponding regions in the bovine AC9 (TM1–6 and TM7–12) shows that the helices TM1–5 (and TM7–11 for the AC9) form a well defined structural motif (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This is observed in structural comparison shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: The TM region that forms the HD helix is swapped in AC9: the TM12 of AC9 occupies the same position as the TM6 of Cya.
source: A striking difference between the Cya and AC9 membrane domains is that the TM region that forms the HD helix is swapped in AC9: the TM12 of AC9 occupies the same position as the TM6 of Cya.
evidence: This is observed in structural comparison.

claim: TM6 in AC9 is placed in a corresponding position relative to the TM7–11.
source: Similarly, TM6 in AC9 is placed in a corresponding position relative to the TM7–11 (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This is observed in structural comparison shown in Figure 2F, G.

claim: The TM1–5 bundle in Cya appears to act as a 'guide rail' for the TM6/HD helix of Cya, guiding the correct assembly of the HD coiled coil and the catalytic domain of the cyclase.
source: The TM1–5 bundle in Cya appears to act as a 'guide rail' for the TM6/HD helix of Cya, guiding the correct assembly of the HD coiled coil and the catalytic domain of the cyclase (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The guide rail feature is remarkably similar in AC9, with TM1–5 and TM7–11 arranged in a near-identical way.
source: This feature is remarkably similar in AC9, with TM1–5 and TM7–11 arranged in a near-identical way (Figure 3B), and with a closely matching HD core (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in structural comparison shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: Previous experiments in M. intracellulare Cya have shown that the HD and the TM regions of the protein are critically important for the protein's dimerization and functional assembly.
source: The previous experiments in M. intracellulare Cya have shown that the HD and the TM regions of the protein are critically important for the protein's dimerization and functional assembly (Vercellino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The lack of the TM region results in failure to form a stable active dimer of M. tuberculosis Rv1625c/Cya.
source: The lack of the TM region results in failure to form a stable active dimer of M. tuberculosis Rv1625c/Cya, even in the presence of a nucleotide analogue MANT-GTP, judged by the inability of MANT-GTP to induce crystallization of the protein in a dimeric form (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is observed in crystallographic experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The soluble domain of the M. intracellulare Cya is effectively dimerized by MANT-GTP.
source: In contrast, the soluble domain of the M. intracellulare Cya is effectively dimerized by MANT-GTP (Vercellino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The isolated Cya-SOL construct can form an inactive domain-swapped dimeric assembly.
source: The importance of the TM domain as a factor that promotes correct protein folding is further illustrated by the ability of the isolated Cya-SOL construct to form an inactive domain-swapped dimeric assembly (Barathy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The key function of the TM domain in a membrane AC is to guide the assembly of the enzyme in a catalytically competent form.
source: It is thus tempting to suggest that the key function of the TM domain in a membrane AC is to guide the assembly of the enzyme in a catalytically competent form.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: In the inactive form of sGC, the HD helices are bent, with an accompanying substantial unwinding of the HD core.
source: In its inactive form, the sGC displays a conformation where HD helices are bent, with an accompanying substantial unwinding of the HD core (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is observed in the structure of inactive sGC shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Activation of sGC is accompanied with a large-scale conformational change, 'straightening' the HD.
source: In contrast, activation of sGC is accompanied with a large-scale conformational change, 'straightening' the HD (Figure 3H) and adopting the HD conformation that closely matches that of Cya (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is observed in the structure of activated sGC shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The position of the 'kink' in the HD of sGC approximately corresponds to the membrane–cytosol interface in Cya.
source: The position of the 'kink' in the HD of sGC approximately corresponds to the membrane–cytosol interface in Cya.
evidence: This is observed in structural comparison.

claim: The very distant yet related proteins sGC and Cya may be subject to very similar modes of regulation involving changes in the HD, which may result in changes in the catalytic domain of the protein.
source: Thus, the very distant yet related proteins sGC and Cya (as well as AC9 and other membrane ACs) may be subject to very similar modes of regulation involving changes in the HD, which may result in changes in the catalytic domain of the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison.

claim: In sGC the regulation process is guided by the heme-containing receptor domain, while in the membrane ACs this function is likely performed by the TM domain.
source: While in sGC the process is guided by the heme-containing receptor domain, in the membrane ACs this function is likely performed by the TM domain.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison and functional considerations.

claim: The structure of Cya revealed several prominent cavities in the TM domain of the protein, which may serve a stabilizing or regulatory role.
source: The structure of Cya revealed several prominent cavities in the TM domain of the protein, which may serve a stabilizing or regulatory role (Figure 4).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: A negatively charged cleft (site Ex1) is formed at the extracellular interface of the two 6-TM bundles.
source: A negatively charged cleft (site Ex1) is formed at the extracellular interface of the two 6-TM bundles (Figure 4A, D, E).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 4A, D, E.

claim: The negative charge of the Ex1 pocket is provided by the residues D123, E164, and D170 of each monomer, facing into the cavity.
source: The negative charge of this pocket is provided by the residues D123, E164, and D170 of each monomer, facing into the cavity (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The Ex1 region may be involved in binding of positively charged ions, small molecules, lipids, or peptides.
source: This region may be involved in binding of positively charged ions, small molecules, lipids, or peptides.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural features of the Ex1 site.

claim: The ability of NB4 nanobody to interact with the Ex1 pocket spuriously indicates that it may also be a site of interaction with a yet unknown natural protein partner.
source: The ability of NB4 nanobody to interact with this pocket spuriously (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) indicates that it may also be a site of interaction with a yet unknown natural protein partner.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of NB4 binding shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A prominent pocket open to the extracellular side of the protein is formed within each TM bundle (site Ex2).
source: Additionally, a prominent pocket open to the extracellular side of the protein is formed within each TM bundle (site Ex2; Figure 4A, C, D).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 4A, C, D.

claim: The Ex2 pocket may accommodate small molecules or lipids, with a possible access route from the outer leaflet of the lipid bilayer surrounding Cya.
source: This pocket may accommodate small molecules or lipids, with a possible access route from the outer leaflet of the lipid bilayer surrounding Cya.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural features of the Ex2 site.

claim: A similar internal pocket is present in the TM1–6 bundle in AC9.
source: A similar internal pocket is present in the TM1–6 bundle in AC9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Deep pockets on the cytosolic side of the Cya TM region are formed between the HD domain and the N-terminus/TM1 (site Cy1), as well as between TM1 and TM3 (site Cy2).
source: Deep pockets on the cytosolic side of the Cya TM region are formed between the HD domain and the N-terminus/TM1 (site Cy1), as well as between TM1 and TM3 (site Cy2; Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 4B–D.

claim: Close to the entrances into the Cy1 and Cy2 pockets are the positively charged residues R43, R44, R46 of the N-terminus, as well as R203 and R207 in the HD domain from the adjacent monomer.
source: Close to the entrances into these pockets are the positively charged residues R43 (Cy1/Cy2), R44 (Cy2), R46 (Cy1) of the N-terminus, as well as R203 and R207 (Cy1) in the HD domain from the adjacent monomer (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The positive charge of the Cy1/Cy2 region indicates a potential role in interactions with the phospholipid headgroups or positively charged peptides or small molecules.
source: The positive charge of this region indicates a potential role in interactions with the phospholipid headgroups or positively charged peptides or small molecules.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural features.

claim: The residues 1–40 of Cya are not resolved in the 3D reconstruction but may interact with and occlude the cytosolic pockets.
source: The interpretation of these cytosolic intramembrane pockets requires caution, as the residues 1–40 of Cya are not resolved in our 3D reconstruction but may interact with and occlude these pockets.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat in interpreting the structure.

claim: Analysis of the area around the sites Ex2–Cy2 shows that they are discontinuous, precluding formation of a channel traversing the entire width of the membrane.
source: Analysis of the area around the sites Ex2–Cy2 shows that they are discontinuous, precluding formation of a channel traversing the entire width of the membrane (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is observed in structural analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MD simulations confirmed the ability of water molecules to enter into the Ex2 and Cy2 site, but no TM water transport could be observed.
source: Our molecular dynamics (MD) simulations confirmed the ability of water molecules to enter into the Ex2 and Cy2 site, but no TM water transport could be observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in MD simulation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The density map features a small but prominent density in the site Ex1, which could correspond to a bound metal or a yet unknown component co-purified with the protein from E. coli.
source: Our density map features a small but prominent density in the site Ex1 (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which presently cannot be assigned to a specific entity, but which could correspond to a bound metal (Na+, Mg2, Mn2, or a yet unknown component co-purified with the protein from E. coli).
evidence: This is observed in the density map shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Disruption of the negatively charged Ex1 interface may lead to the loss of the rail structure of the TM region, with concomitant changes in the HD helix arrangement and ultimately the catalytic domain of Cya.
source: It is conceivable that disruption of this negatively charged interface may lead to the loss of the rail structure of the TM region, with concomitant changes in the HD helix arrangement and ultimately the catalytic domain of Cya.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural considerations.

claim: MD simulations showed that the site Ex1 behaved as a genuine metal-binding site, occupied by the K+ and Mg2+ ions similar to the metal-binding site in the Cya catalytic centre over the course of the simulation.
source: The site Ex1 behaved as a genuine metal-binding site, occupied by the K+ and Mg2+ ions similar to the metal-binding site in the Cya catalytic centre over the course of the simulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B–E).
evidence: This is shown in MD simulation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B–E.

claim: The evidence obtained experimentally and using MD simulations strongly supports a function of the extracellular surface of Cya as a receptor for positively charged ligands.
source: Thus, the evidence obtained experimentally and using MD simulations strongly supports a function of the extracellular surface of Cya as a receptor for positively charged ligands.
evidence: This is concluded based on experimental and simulation data.

claim: The Ex1-5A mutant was successfully expressed and purified in digitonin.
source: The resulting construct (referred to as Ex1-5A, Figure 5A, C) was successfully expressed and purified in digitonin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in purification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The thermostability profiles of the Ex1-5A mutant in the absence or in the presence of a nucleotide were similar to those of the wild-type Cya.
source: The thermostability profiles of the Ex1-5A mutant in the absence or in the presence of a nucleotide were similar to those of the wild-type Cya (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is shown in thermostability data in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The enzymatic activity of Ex1-5A was substantially reduced with a dramatic increase in apparent Km.
source: In contrast, the enzymatic activity of Ex1-5A was substantially reduced (with a dramatic increase in apparent Km, Figure 5E), with a fourfold reduction in apparent affinity for a nucleotide inhibitor, MANT-GTP (judged by the MANT-GTP IC50 values, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in activity assay data in Figure 5E.

claim: The Ex1-5A mutant showed a fourfold reduction in apparent affinity for MANT-GTP.
source: In contrast, the enzymatic activity of Ex1-5A was substantially reduced (with a dramatic increase in apparent Km, Figure 5E), with a fourfold reduction in apparent affinity for a nucleotide inhibitor, MANT-GTP (judged by the MANT-GTP IC50 values, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in inhibition data in Figure 5F.

claim: LiP-MS analysis revealed a significant increase in protease accessibility of the HD in the Ex1-5A mutant.
source: Comparative analysis of the LiP-MS profile of the wild-type Cya and the Ex1-5A mutant revealed a significant increase in protease accessibility of the HD in the mutant (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This is shown in LiP-MS data in Figure 5G, H.

claim: Modification of the extracellular site Ex1 of Cya leads to changes in the dynamics of its cytosolic HD, accompanied by a dramatic reduction in enzymatic activity.
source: Thus, modification of the extracellular site Ex1 of Cya leads to changes in the dynamics of its cytosolic HD, accompanied by a dramatic reduction in enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is concluded based on LiP-MS and activity assay data.

claim: Only two of the site Ex1 residues are well conserved (T122 and Q127), based on the alignment of 180 close homologues of Cya.
source: Interestingly, only two of the site Ex1 residues are well conserved, based on the alignment of 180 close homologues of Cya (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3A): while T122 and Q127 are relatively well conserved, the residues D123, E164, and D170 are not.
evidence: This is shown in conservation analysis in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3A.

claim: The residues D123, E164, and D170 in the Ex1 site are not well conserved among Cya homologues.
source: Interestingly, only two of the site Ex1 residues are well conserved, based on the alignment of 180 close homologues of Cya (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3A): while T122 and Q127 are relatively well conserved, the residues D123, E164, and D170 are not.
evidence: This is shown in conservation analysis in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3A.

claim: The site Ex2 is lined by largely nonconserved residues.
source: Likewise, the site Ex2 is lined by largely nonconserved residues (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in conservation analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: MD simulations with Ex1-5A protein revealed a dramatic difference between the B factors of the Ex1-5A and the wild-type protein, indicative of increased conformational flexibility of the mutant.
source: The simulation revealed a dramatic difference between the B factors of the Ex1-5A and the wild-type protein, indicative of increased conformational flexibility of the mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in MD simulation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Metal ion binding was preserved at the cytosolic domain of the Ex1-5A, but was completely disrupted at the extracellular Ex1 site.
source: As expected, metal ion binding was preserved at the cytosolic domain of the Ex1-5A, but was completely disrupted at the extracellular Ex1 site (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is shown in MD simulation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: The TM1–5 region may be more conformationally flexible in the Ex1-5A mutant.
source: Analysis of the distances between select residues in Cya and in Ex1-5A showed that although the core remains relatively stable for both protein, the TM1–5 region may be more conformationally flexible (judged by the increased average distances between the residues A77–A77 and L92–L92 within the dimer; Figure 5—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This is shown in MD simulation data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D, E.

claim: Disruption of the extracellular surface of Cya (site Ex1) leads to profound changes within the intramembrane part of the protein, as well as at a distant catalytic domain.
source: Together with the functional data, the results of the MD simulations strongly suggest that disruption of the extracellular surface of Cya (site Ex1) leads to profound changes within the intramembrane part of the protein, as well as at a distant catalytic domain.
evidence: This is concluded based on MD simulation and functional data.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of M. tuberculosis Cya provides a unique insight into the assembly and regulation of a model membrane AC.
source: The cryo-EM structure of M. tuberculosis Cya provides a unique insight into the assembly and regulation of a model membrane AC.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: The TM domain of ACs facilitates the assembly of the HD domain.
source: Our structure provides two possible reasons for the ACs to have such a TM domain: (1) to facilitate the assembly of the HD domain and (2) to act as a receptor module, binding ligands at several newly identified putative ligand-binding sites, including the pockets within the Cya monomers and at the Cya–Cya interface (Figure 6).
evidence: This is concluded based on structural analysis and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The TM domain of ACs acts as a receptor module, binding ligands at several newly identified putative ligand-binding sites.
source: Our structure provides two possible reasons for the ACs to have such a TM domain: (1) to facilitate the assembly of the HD domain and (2) to act as a receptor module, binding ligands at several newly identified putative ligand-binding sites, including the pockets within the Cya monomers and at the Cya–Cya interface (Figure 6).
evidence: This is concluded based on structural analysis and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: The two functions of the TM domain (assembly facilitation and receptor function) are not mutually exclusive.
source: The two functions are not mutually exclusive, as the ligand interactions with the membrane region of the AC may influence the HD assembly and thus regulate the cyclase function.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Previous work utilizing chimeric constructs revealed that the membrane anchors of the ACs may act as orphan receptors for yet unknown ligands.
source: Previous work utilizing chimeric constructs composed of fragments of the quorum sensing receptor CqsS from Vibrio harveyi and Cya (Beltz et al., 2016) or mammalian membrane ACs (Seth et al., 2020) revealed that the membrane anchors of the ACs may act as orphan receptors for yet unknown ligands.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The structure described here is consistent with the findings that membrane anchors of ACs may act as orphan receptors.
source: Together with the proposed functional coupling between the TM domain and the catalytic site of Cya, the structure described here is consistent with these findings, offering molecular insights into the potential receptor role of the membrane anchor of a model membrane AC.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion connecting the current findings with previous work.

claim: The properties of the Ex1 site are strongly suggestive of a specific ligand-binding site.
source: However, the properties of the Ex1 site are strongly suggestive of a specific ligand-binding site, with a cluster of 10 polar residues (6 negatively charged residues) at the Cya dimer interface pointing towards the Ex1 cavity.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: The most telling evidence for the role of the Ex1 site in cation binding is the MD simulation, which revealed two locations on the Cya surface where the metal ions dwell: the established metal-binding site in the catalytic pocket, and the site Ex1.
source: The most telling evidence for the role of this site in cation binding is the MD simulation, which revealed two locations on the Cya surface where the metal ions dwell: the established metal-binding site in the catalytic pocket, and the site Ex1.
evidence: This is concluded based on MD simulation data.

claim: The Ex1 site at the extracellular surface of the protein likely plays a pivotal role in controlling the assembly of the catalytically active dimeric Cya.
source: Modification of the charges of the Ex1 by mutagenesis reduced the activity of the protein, further suggesting that this site at the extracellular surface of the protein likely plays a pivotal role in controlling the assembly of the catalytically active dimeric Cya.
evidence: This is concluded based on mutagenesis and activity data.

claim: Sensing of extracellular metals is well established in eukaryotic and prokaryotic cell signalling.
source: It is worth noting that sensing of extracellular metals is well established in eukaryotic and prokaryotic cell signalling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) is a GPCR involved in regulation of Ca2+ homeostasis in mammalian signalling.
source: For example, a prominent example in mammalian signalling pathway is the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), a GPCR involved in regulation of Ca2+ homeostasis (Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Salt sensing has been shown in histidine kinases (Sphingomonas melonis KipF) in bacteria.
source: In bacteria, salt sensing has been shown in histidine kinases (Sphingomonas melonis KipF) (Kaczmarczyk et al., 2015) and in chemotaxis receptors (E. coli Tar) (Bi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Salt sensing has been shown in chemotaxis receptors (E. coli Tar) in bacteria.
source: In bacteria, salt sensing has been shown in histidine kinases (Sphingomonas melonis KipF) (Kaczmarczyk et al., 2015) and in chemotaxis receptors (E. coli Tar) (Bi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: A potential link between extracellular metal ion sensing and cAMP signalling that may be mediated by the M. tuberculosis Cya is within the realm of possibility.
source: Thus, a potential link between extracellular metal ion sensing and cAMP signalling that may be mediated by the M. tuberculosis Cya is within the realm of possibility and presents an interesting avenue for future investigations.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative conclusion.

claim: The presence of potential ligand-binding pockets at the extracellular surface of Cya lends strong support to the idea that the TM domains of the ACs may act as receptor modules for yet unknown ligands.
source: The presence of potential ligand-binding pockets at the extracellular surface of Cya lends strong support to the long-standing idea that the TM domains of the ACs may act as receptor modules for yet unknown ligands (Beltz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is concluded based on structural findings and supported by citation.

claim: Direct modulation of the cAMP production through the AC membrane domains could revolutionize the approaches to drug development for a wide range of diseases where the GPCRs are currently the primary drug targets.
source: Direct modulation of the cAMP production through the AC membrane domains could revolutionize the approaches to drug development for a wide range of diseases where the GPCRs are currently the primary drug targets.
evidence: This is stated as a potential implication of the findings.

claim: Interactions between existing drugs and the membrane domains of the ACs may lead to unwanted side effects associated with cAMP signalling.
source: A related notion of importance for molecular pharmacology and medicinal chemistry is the potential interactions between the already existing drugs and the membrane domains of the ACs. Such interactions may lead to unwanted side effects associated with cAMP signalling, such as emesis and changes in heart rate and contractility (Parnell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a potential implication and supported by citation.

claim: The antifungal drug miconazole is known to have cardiotoxic effects.
source: An example of this is the antifungal drug miconazole, which is known to have cardiotoxic effects (Fainstein and Bodey, 1980; Won et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Miconazole has been shown to directly activate AC9, likely via its TM domain.
source: Miconazole has recently been shown to directly activate AC9, likely via its TM domain (Simpson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The interaction of miconazole with AC9 may contribute to the cardiorespiratory side effects of this drug.
source: The interaction with AC9 may contribute to the cardiorespiratory side effects of this drug.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited findings.

claim: The closest example of cyclase modulation through the receptor-mediated effect on the HD helices is the case of soluble GC.
source: The closest example of cyclase modulation through the receptor-mediated effect on the HD helices is the case of soluble GC, described at atomic resolution, has been detailed above (Figure 3; Kang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison and supported by citation and Figure 3.

claim: The presence of disease-linked mutations in the HD regions of AC5 and retGC1 underscore the importance of this domain for cyclase structure and function.
source: The presence of disease-linked mutations in the HD regions of AC5 (Chen et al., 2012; Carecchio et al., 2017) and retGC1 (Tucker et al., 2004; Zhao et al., 2013) underscore the importance of this domain for cyclase structure and function.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The HD region plays a vital part in AC and GC assembly and stability.
source: It is clear that the HD region plays a vital part in AC and GC assembly and stability.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The MD simulations and the experiments with the Ex1-5A mutant of Cya are suggestive of a receptor–transducer–catalyst relay.
source: Our MD simulations and the experiments with the Ex1-5A mutant of Cya are suggestive of a receptor–transducer–catalyst relay, where the extracellular portion of the TM region acts as a 'receptor' for a yet unknown ligand, the HD transduces the activation, and the catalytic domain catalyses ATP to cAMP conversion.
evidence: This is concluded based on MD simulations and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Previous work on Cya identified the HD region as a transducer of a putative signal.
source: This notion is further supported by previous work on Cya that identified the HD region as a transducer of a putative signal (Beltz et al., 2016; Ziegler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The structure of Cya can serve as a starting point for exploration of the TM domain-mediated regulation of membrane ACs.
source: The structure of Cya can serve as a starting point for exploration of the TM domain-mediated regulation of membrane ACs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the utility of the structure.
